extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, constitutional history, and comparative government
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing normative principles and institutional criteria for stable constitutional government as discussed through ancient examples (Rome, Sparta, Carthage, Germanic tribes, Homeric polities). Emphasizes balance, separation of powers, voting mechanisms, and social/economic conditions that affect constitutional stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most perfect form = mixture of monarchy, aristocracy, democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The most perfect form of government consists of an equal mixture of monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy (as stated by Dionysius/Polybius).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited as a normative ideal and illustrated by Polybius and Lycurgus; Rome and Sparta approached this mixture, which is credited for their long duration and strong effects on character. Used as an evaluative standard: systems approximating this mixture are judged superior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three orders required for a stable balance
rubrics_metrics.description: A durable balance requires three distinct orders — king (monarchy), nobles/senate (aristocracy), and the people (democracy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated argument: no government of laws without a balance, no balance without three orders. Examples: failures occur when only two centers of power struggle (king vs senate, or senate vs people).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of each order in its department
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of the three orders must be independent and absolute within its own department to maintain equilibrium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that three orders can never balance unless each is independent and has absolute authority in its proper sphere; lack of such independence leads to domination by one order (e.g., oligarchy or tyranny).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers with mutual negatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive should be separated from legislative, judicial from both, and king, senate, and people should each have a negative (veto) in the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an obvious improvement on earlier constitutions; absence of separation and negative powers allowed senates or factions to dominate. Practical examples: Romulus's constitution lacked clear negatives, enabling senate dominance over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware annually elective small bodies — they become factional instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Small elective bodies chosen annually (e.g., a council of five) are changeable and easily captured by the prevailing faction, undermining constitutional stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from Carthage: making a small council annually elective turned it into an instrument 'always in the hands of the prevailing faction' and contributed to overturning the constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voting method determines real power (curiae vs centuries)
rubrics_metrics.description: How votes are taken (by curiae/tribes vs by centuries/wealth-classes) crucially affects which social group holds power; weighted systems can make the rich predominant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tullius's change from voting by curiae (where the many plebeians prevail) to voting by centuries (weighted by property) shifted power to the rich patricians. Evaluative guidance: choose voting mechanisms that reflect intended representation and avoid structural weighting that marginalizes the majority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchy must be limited and defined in function
rubrics_metrics.description: Kings should have clear, limited functions (supremacy in religion, guardian of laws, administration of justice in great cases, assembling senate and people, delivering first opinion), and must not be absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Romulus's defined functions are given as a model of limited monarchy. The text cautions against absolute kings and Spartan oddities (two kings). Evaluative point: assess whether a monarch's duties are constrained and institutionalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent hereditary monopolization of offices and honors
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalities of election that mask hereditary transmission of offices and honors (nobility, dukes, counts) produce aristocratic monopolies and erode genuine accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tacitus's account of Germanic/feudal hierarchies shows titles and powers descending in families despite nominal election. Criterion: check whether elections are substantive or merely confirm hereditary dominance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create effective popular checks (tribunes/representatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the people lack independence, establish institutional representatives (e.g., tribunes) or assemblies with enforceable checks so popular rights are meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roman history: tribunate established after tyranny and oligarchic abuses; mere theoretical privileges (choose magistrates, enact laws, determine war) are insufficient without real enforcement. Evaluative emphasis on institutional empowerment of popular bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic protections to preserve citizens' political independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Protect citizens from debt slavery and crippling economic burdens, because economic subjugation (e.g., debt bondage to creditors) destroys popular independence and fuels instability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: plebeians forced to serve at their own expense, borrow at exorbitant interest, and be enslaved for debts — this produced demands for abolition of debts and social conflict. Criterion: evaluate laws on debt and economic burdens for their political effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentration of military/command power that enables usurpation
rubrics_metrics.description: When the three orders fail to balance, ambitious military leaders can grab power (e.g., Caesar); constitutions must prevent concentration of armed authority in single individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical trajectory: popular-senate struggles opened the path for Caesar's usurpation. Institutional checks on commanders, civil control of armies, and divided authority reduce risk of personal rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberative procedure in assemblies must be clear and not merely theatrical
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemblies need regular meeting rules, clear vote counts, and genuine deliberation; reliance on noisy assent (clash of arms, murmurs) or nobles dominating speech yields hollow popular decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tacitus on Germanic assemblies: people assembled irregularly, nobles spoke, votes expressed by noise, not counted—thus assemblies functioned to proclaim elite decisions rather than check them. Evaluation should examine procedural clarity and voice-counting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the power of symbolic/religious legitimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets, priests, and religious beliefs can confer legitimacy on rulers (divine descent, sacred rites), and such symbolic authority can override legal constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Roman and Greek bards and poets propagating kings' divine ancestry (Odyssean bards supporting kings), and Germanic priests' authority in assemblies. Evaluative attention: assess non-legal sources of authority that affect constitutional functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patron-client networks preserve order but entrench aristocratic influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems where plebeians choose patrician patrons in exchange for clientage create reciprocal obligations that can preserve peace but also serve to entrench aristocratic dominance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Romulus's patron-client institution produced civility and harmony for centuries but also tied plebeians into dependence on patricians. Criterion: weigh social cohesion benefits against long-term political inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional forms must guard against factional family rivalry
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutions should limit the ability of noble families to divide into competing factions that seize state instruments; otherwise family factionalism will perpetually destabilize government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roman narrative: noble families (Hanno vs Barcas in Carthage; patrician families in Rome) used institutions to fight for supremacy, producing instability. Evaluate whether institutional rules reduce family- faction capture (term limits, broader eligibility, impartial procedures).
